true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid webhook body returns an unhandled 500

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` throws a ZodError for malformed request bodies and there is no try/catch around it. A caller with the correct webhook secret can trigger a 500 and default error page instead of a controlled 400 validation response. Use `safeParse` and return the validation error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential find-first then create/update can create duplicates

The endpoint looks up an existing credential with `findFirst` and then either updates or creates it. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user/app can both observe no existing row and both insert, leaving duplicate credentials. Since credential selection elsewhere may rely on a single row per user/app, this can cause ambiguity. The operation should be serialized under a transaction/unique constraint or the insert should be idempotent.

Encryption key generation command does not produce a 32-byte key

The comment says CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY must be 32 bytes for AES256, but suggests `openssl rand -base64 24`. That command encodes 24 random bytes as a 32-character base64 string; if decoded for use as the AES key it is only 24 bytes, and if used directly as a string the comment is still misleading. Use `openssl rand -base64 32` (which encodes a 32-byte key) instead.

Salesforce refresh token flow runs on every CalendarService construction

`getClient` performs an OAuth refresh request and credential update every time a SalesforceCalendarService instance is created, regardless of whether the stored token is still valid. This adds an external API call and database write for each booking operation and may hit Salesforce rate limits. It should refresh only when the token is near or past expiry, or use jsforce's built-in refresh behavior.

Zoom refresh sends wrong appSlug

The Zoom app id/slug is `zoom` everywhere else in this package (callback uses `appId: "zoom"` and redirects to `slug: "zoom"`), but credential-sync mode sends `appSlug: "zoomvideo"`. A self-hosted app store keyed by the actual Cal.com app slug will not match the Zoom integration.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Guest email comparisons are case-sensitive, bypassing blacklist and duplicate checks

`BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS` is split and lowercased, but each `guest` is compared as supplied. A guest address such as `User@Example.com` will bypass `user@example.com`. In addition, the comparison against existing `booking.attendees` is case-sensitive, so the same email with different case can be added more than once. Normalize guest emails before filtering and deduplicating.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check requires both admin and owner roles

The code computes `isTeamAdminOrOwner` as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. That makes the action available only to users who are both a team admin and a team owner, which is normally impossible. A user who is only an admin or only an owner is denied, despite the variable name and the UI exposing the action to `booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`. This should use `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unbounded and duplicate guest list accepted at API

`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.max()` and no uniqueness constraint. A direct tRPC caller can submit an arbitrarily large list, causing a large `createMany`, many external calendar API updates, and many invitation emails in one request. Add a sane maximum and reject duplicate entries at the schema or handler level.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New add-guests emails ignore event-type email suppression settings

`sendAddGuestsEmails` does not receive or check `eventTypeMetadata` and always sends organizer, team-member, and attendee emails. Other comparable functions (`sendLocationChangeEmails`, `sendScheduledEmails`) honor `eventTypeDisableHostEmail` and `eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail`. As a result, event types configured to disable host or attendee emails will still emit these notifications when guests are added.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Database commit before external calendar update leaves unretryable partial state

The new attendees are written to Postgres at line 92 before `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` on line 165. That external call is not covered by a try/catch or transaction, so if it fails the request errors while the new attendees remain. Retrying then sees them as already existing (`uniqueGuests.length === 0`) and returns `BAD_REQUEST`, so the booking can be left permanently out of sync unless rows are manually removed. Add compensation handling or perform/validate the calendar update before committing, and make retries idempotent.

External calendar update uses caller credentials instead of booking organizer credentials

`EventManager` is constructed with `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)`. Since attendees and team admins/owners are allowed to call this handler, the credentials belong to the caller, not the owner of the booking/destination calendar. For such callers the calendar event is likely not updated or an update is attempted against the wrong account. The handler even fetches `booking.user.credentials` but never uses them. Use the booking organizer's credentials for `EventManager`.

No status or end-time check: guests can be added to past bookings

The handler only checks that the booking exists and that the caller has some role; it never rejects past bookings or disallowed statuses. The UI also includes the add-guests action under edit for past confirmed bookings (`apps/web/components/booking/BookingListItem.tsx` line 554). This allows new invitations and external calendar updates for events that have already ended. Reject bookings whose end time has passed and disallowed statuses.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount increments are not atomic

Both update sites use `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1` based on the value read earlier by `findMany`. If two cron invocations overlap, they can both read the same value and write the same value, losing an increment. This can defeat the delete-after-two-failures logic and may allow more retries or duplicate Twilio schedule calls than intended. Use an atomic `increment: 1` update instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-count delete branch can delete non-SMS reminders

The new second OR branch only checks `retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, unlike the first branch which filters `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`. `WorkflowReminder` is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP methods, so any non-SMS reminder with `retryCount > 1` would be deleted by this SMS cron job. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and likely `scheduled: false`) to this branch to prevent deleting unrelated workflow reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
All errors count as SMS scheduling failures

The try block includes reminder preparation work such as `getBookerBaseUrl` (line 119) and `bookingMetadataSchema.parse` (line 134) before Twilio is called. The catch at line 190 increments `retryCount` for any error in that block. As a result, a record with malformed booking metadata can throw during parsing each run, reach retryCount 2, and then be deleted at the start of a later run even though no SMS scheduling was ever attempted and the event is still upcoming. Only `twilio.scheduleSMS` failures should count toward this deletion limit, or preparation errors should be handled separately.

true_positives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Org authorization omits user bookings when org has no child teams

buildOrgAuthorizationCondition only queries userIdsFromOrg when teamsFromOrg.length > 0. An organization can have accepted members via the org membership itself even when it has no child teams, but in that case the isTeamBooking = false branch is omitted entirely. As a result, an org owner/admin cannot see personal/user-scoped bookings of org members for organizations without child teams. The guard should not depend on teamsFromOrg.length, or the membership query should still run with [options.orgId].

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

false_positives.candidate:
Org/team raw SQL branches are never executed against the database

The team and org authorization tests only assert that the generated Prisma.sql object equals an expected Prisma.sql object. They do not run a query using those conditions, so a SQL syntax error, invalid ANY(array) parameter binding, or incorrect column/table mapping in the org/team OR branches would not be caught. The only end-to-end query test uses user scope. Consider adding a $queryRaw execution for at least one team or org branch where the generated SQL is actually sent to the database.

Public options type makes invalid team scope calls compile

InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions declares teamId optional for every scope, whereas the zod schema still requires teamId when scope is 'team'. This means new InsightsBookingService({ scope: 'team', userId, orgId }) now compiles, then safeParse fails in the constructor and the service silently returns NOTHING_CONDITION. This moves a real configuration error from compile time to runtime. The public type should remain a discriminated union or otherwise require teamId for scope 'team'.

Removal of findMany breaks existing callers

The previous public method findMany(findManyArgs) was removed and replaced with getBaseConditions(). Only the service and its integration tests are updated in this PR, so any existing consumer of InsightsBookingService.findMany() will fail TypeScript compilation or, if untyped, throw at runtime. If the raw-SQL conversion is intentional, the same PR should either migrate all call sites or keep a findMany wrapper that builds a raw query from getBaseConditions().

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateMany with an empty data object cannot bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt

`SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})` passes an empty data object to Prisma `updateMany`. Prisma rejects empty update data or produces no real update, so it will not update `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` as the comment claims, and it may throw. This runs after availability cache is written in `fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`, so a throw here can fail the Google webhook/cache-refresh path after cache was already updated. Pass a concrete field such as `{ updatedAt: new Date() }` if the timestamp bump is intended, or remove the call if it is not needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache status query includes expired calendar cache entries

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` groups all CalendarCache rows for the given credential IDs without filtering on `expiresAt`. The actual cache lookup in `getCachedAvailability` only uses rows where `expiresAt >= now()`, so the new UI can report that cache exists for a credential whose cached entries are expired and would not be served. Add `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }` to the `where` clause so the status matches effective cache data.

Passing optional/null cacheUpdatedAt to Date constructor is not type-safe

`cacheUpdatedAt` is declared as `Date | null | undefined`, but `new Date(cacheUpdatedAt)` is called after only checking the separate `hasCache` boolean. TypeScript does not narrow `cacheUpdatedAt` through an aliased boolean check, so with strict null checks this is a compile error; the code is also not type-safe as written. Use a narrowed local value after checking `isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt` directly, or pass a non-null assertion/cast, before constructing the Date.

deleteCache success does not invalidate connectedCalendars query

The delete-cache mutation only calls `onSuccess?.()` and shows a toast. It does not invalidate `trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`, unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component which invalidates that query in `onSettled`. As a result, after deleting cached data the `cacheUpdatedAt` already loaded in the UI remains stale, so the cache status and delete action are still shown until a manual refetch. Add `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()` in the delete mutation's success or settled handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Workflow reminder cancellation is fire-and-forget

deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are async, but their promises are not collected or awaited. The previous code at least awaited the Prisma deletes. As a result, the handler can return success before Twilio/SendGrid cancellation and DB cleanup complete, and failures are swallowed with no retry. Collect the promises and await them before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Immediate SendGrid cancellation leaves no retry state

When immediateDelete is true, the function sends the SendGrid cancellation request and returns without deleting the workflowReminder or setting cancelled=true. If the request fails, the caught error is only logged, the row remains with cancelled null, and the regular CRON cancellation query will never retry it because it is not marked cancelled. For rescheduled bookings this can still allow the old scheduled email to be sent after a transient SendGrid error. Set cancelled=true before attempting the immediate cancellation or delete the row only after success with retry semantics.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Old workflow reminders are cancelled before reschedule succeeds

The new block cancels/deletes the original booking's workflow reminders before calling eventManager.reschedule and before checking whether it succeeded. If reschedule fails, the original booking remains but its reminders are already gone, so the user no longer receives the reminders they should still get. Only cancel old reminders after a successful reschedule, or recreate them on failure.

Paid bookings return before scheduled workflow reminders are cancelled

The paid/refund branch returns at line 464 before the updatedBookings workflow-reminder cancellation block at lines 484-493. Scheduled BEFORE_EVENT/AFTER_EVENT reminders for paid bookings are left untouched and can still be sent after the booking is cancelled/rejected. Move the workflow-reminder cancellation before this early return or restructure the early return.

Past reminders are deleted before cancelled reminders are cancelled

The handler first deletes all EMAIL workflowReminders with scheduledDate <= now (lines 34-41), then later queries for cancelled reminders to cancel at SendGrid (lines 44-51). A reminder cancelled shortly before its scheduledDate can therefore be removed by the first deleteMany when the next 15-minute cron tick runs after the scheduledDate, and the SendGrid scheduled send is never told to cancel, so the unwanted email can still be sent. Cancel processing should run before the past-date deletion, or near-term cancellations should be sent to SendGrid immediately.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recurring calendar deletions are not awaited and can be missed

The recurring cancellation branch uses `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. `forEach` ignores the returned promise, so execution reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at line 652 before these async callbacks have resumed and populated `apiDeletes`. Recurring booking calendar events may never be deleted before the handler returns, and any rejected `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent` promise is unhandled. This regressed because the callback previously used synchronous `getCalendar` and pushed into `apiDeletes` synchronously. Use `for...of` or `Promise.all` and await the deletions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Reschedule cancellation runs in unawaited async forEach

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` does not await the async callbacks. The mutation continues to send reschedule emails and webhooks and can return before the old calendar/video events are cancelled; rejections from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` also become unhandled. Use an actual `for...of`/`Promise.all` and await before sending the follow-up emails.

Storing `import()` promises still eagerly loads every app

Each property is an executed `import()` call, so when this module is evaluated all app modules start loading/evaluating even if no caller ever accesses that app. That undercuts the intended lazy loading and can cause a large prefetch/cold-start cost; an import failure for an unused app can also become an unhandled rejection. Store thunks (e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`) and invoke them at the lookup sites if on-demand loading is desired.

Unawaited async forEach can leave Vital calendar events uncancelled

The async callback passed to `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach` awaits `getCalendar` but `forEach` does not await the returned promise. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from the async callback, and `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` runs before the cancellation work completes. Replace this with a `for...of` loop or collect and `await Promise.all(...)` for the cancellation promises.

Unawaited async forEach can leave WipeMyCal calendar events uncancelled

Same issue as in the vital reschedule helper: the async callback passed to `forEach` is not awaited, so the function can send reschedule emails and return before `getCalendar`/`deleteEvent` finish. Errors from the async callback are unhandled. Use an `await`-able loop or `Promise.all`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end time is computed from slot start, not slot end

The working-hours validation sets both start and end to slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(). The end value should be derived from slotEndTime or at least start + eventLength. As written, a slot that starts inside the host's working hours but ends after the working-hours end passes the check. If the fixed host has shorter availability than the aggregate availability used to generate slots, bookings can be made outside that host's actual working hours.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date override check compares Dayjs objects with ===

The condition dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes") compares two distinct Dayjs object references, so it is always false. A zero-length date override used to mark a date unavailable does not block a slot that starts exactly at that override time, because the callback returns undefined and dateOverrideExist then returns true.

false_positives.candidate:
Date overrides bypass busy checks, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot is not excluded by the override, the function returns true at line 133 before running the busy.every conflict check. This means calendar bookings and existing Cal bookings for that host are ignored on any day with a date override, so a slot can be offered even when the host is already busy. This applies to fixed hosts and regular non-team event hosts, leading to double-bookings on override days.

Multiple same-day date overrides are not all considered

The dateOverrides.find callback sets dateOverrideExist and returns true immediately when it finds a same-day override that does not contain the slot. If a host has several date-override intervals on the same date, a slot that lies in a later interval is rejected because an earlier same-day interval returned true first. The logic should determine whether the slot is inside any of the same-day overrides rather than stopping at the first one that excludes it.

No regression test for fixed-host date overrides in round-robin

The PR's main round-robin fix is that fixed-host date overrides are now enforced in availableTimeSlots through checkIfIsAvailable, but the only added test covers a personal event date override with a different timezone. There is no test creating a round-robin event with one fixed host, a date override for that fixed host, and a round-robin host. That is the most complex new path and should have a regression test.

Timezone-adjusted date overrides drop day-crossing information

The active-override filter at line 206 still uses dayjs.utc(override.start), and the start/end calculation at lines 219-224 only keeps hour() and minute() after adding the offset. When the organizer/invitee timezone adjustment crosses midnight, this discards the new day. For example, a 23:30-23:45 Honolulu override is 02:30-02:45 next day in Los Angeles, but the current code can attach the override to the previous invitee day and produce 02:30 without carrying into the next day. This makes date overrides near midnight appear on the wrong day in certain timezones.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Direct metadata indexing can raise KeyError for integrations without sender

`integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` assumes every active Integration has a `sender` dict with `login`. However `build_integration` only sets `metadata["sender"]` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy, and the pipeline state does not populate `sender`, so integrations created through this fallback (and older rows) may lack it. When this branch is reached for such an Integration, the request raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended installation error page. Use `.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and handle a missing value explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
GitHub installer validation is skipped when Integration row does not exist yet

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the first `except Integration.DoesNotExist` immediately returns `pipeline.next_step()`. This means if the GitHub installation webhook has not yet created the `Integration` row when the browser completes the Sentry setup pipeline (or if it never does), the sender check is bypassed completely. The pipeline then proceeds to `build_integration`, which uses the app JWT to fetch the installation by user-supplied `installation_id` and creates the Integration without `metadata.sender`. An attacker with a Sentry session and a known/guessed `installation_id` can therefore link a GitHub installation to their Sentry organization without being the GitHub user who installed it. The check should fail closed in this path, or `build_integration` should require/derive and store the installer and validate it.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AssignmentSource.queued uses import-time default instead of creation time

queued: datetime = timezone.now() is evaluated once when the module is imported. Every AssignmentSource constructed without an explicit queued argument, including from_integration, therefore gets the module import time rather than the time the source was created. If queued is intended to track when the assignment source was queued or generated, use field(default_factory=timezone.now) from dataclasses so each instance is stamped at construction time.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for same-source deassign suppression

There is a test for assign with a matching source integration, but the inbound deassign path also passes AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration) in sync_group_assignee_inbound and should be suppressed by the same should_sync check. A Jira unassign webhook would still echo back to Jira if this path regresses or fails to propagate the source. Add a test where GroupAssignee.objects.deassign is called with a matching AssignmentSource and assert sync_assignee_outbound is not called.

Same-integration suppression is overbroad for groups linked to multiple external issues

should_sync now returns False whenever the assignment source's integration_id matches the target organization integration. AssignmentSource only carries integration_id, not the specific external issue that triggered the inbound change. sync_assignee_outbound uses the same assignment_source_dict for every GroupLink for the group, so if a group is linked to multiple external issues in the same integration, an inbound assignment from one of those issues suppresses outbound sync to all of them. The other linked issues in that integration will remain on the old assignee. The source should include the originating external issue key and the check should suppress only that external issue, or otherwise avoid suppressing unrelated linked issues.

should_sync is now called with an extra argument that existing overrides may not accept

The task now calls installation.should_sync("outbound_assignee", parsed_assignment_source). Previously should_sync was defined and overridden as should_sync(self, attribute). Any integration subclass that still overrides should_sync with the old single-argument signature will raise TypeError when outbound assignee sync runs, causing the task to fail and retry for that integration. All overrides must be updated or the task must call this without a second positional argument unless it knows the installation can accept it.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is abstract and cannot be instantiated

StatefulDetectorHandler declares abstract methods counter_names, get_dedupe_value, get_group_key_values, and build_occurrence_and_event_data. MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from it with pass and implements none of them, so it remains an abstract class. MetricAlertFire.detector_handler points to this abstract class, and Detector.detector_handler does group_type.detector_handler(self), so processing any Detector with type 'metric_alert_fire' will raise TypeError when trying to instantiate it. Either implement the stateful detector methods or keep this as a plain DetectorHandler stub until the stateful implementation exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate docstring still says it returns a list

The evaluate method now returns dict[DetectorGroupKey, DetectorEvaluationResult], but its docstring still says it returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult. This is misleading for implementers and callers and should be updated to match the new contract.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.

false_positives.candidate:
Test builds expected occurrence with the wrong group key

In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built with group key 'val1', but the evaluate_group_key_value call under test uses group key 'group_key'. The handler's build_occurrence_and_event_data uses the group key it receives to build the fingerprint, so the actual occurrence fingerprint will be '<detector_id>:group_key' while the expected occurrence fingerprint is '<detector_id>:val1'. DetectorEvaluationResult equality compares the result field, so this assertion will fail. Build the expected occurrence with 'group_key' or change the evaluation to use 'val1' consistently.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Monitor context returns original config instead of the modified copy

`get_monitor_environment_context` copies `monitor_environment.monitor.config` into `config` and, when `schedule_type` is present, replaces it with the display value. However the returned dict uses `monitor_environment.monitor.config` on line 168, not the modified `config`. The copy and display conversion are dead code, so `schedule_type` is emitted as the raw stored value (for example an int/enum) instead of the intended display string in the occurrence context.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Incident can be triggered before reaching failure_issue_threshold

For `failure_issue_threshold > 1`, the code slices the latest `failure_issue_threshold` check-ins but does not verify that there actually are that many. On a new or sparse monitor, after the first failed check-in `previous_checkins` contains only that one failure; the `any(... == CheckInStatus.OK)` check is false, so the monitor is set to ERROR and an incident is created even though the configured consecutive-failure threshold has not been met. This defeats the user-configured threshold and can cause premature monitor alerts.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join(timeout) can return while later flusher processes are still running

In `join`, after `next_step.join(timeout)` consumes the deadline, the loop over `self.processes` sees `remaining_time <= 0` and executes `break`, skipping termination for the current and all remaining processes. Only processes iterated before the deadline expires are terminated. Because `close()` intentionally leaves flusher processes running until `join()`, this can leave an old generation of flusher processes alive after rebalance, concurrently flushing shards that may now be assigned to a new consumer and producing duplicate buffered segments.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Inserting flusher_processes before produce_to_pipe breaks positional callers

`ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` previously accepted `produce_to_pipe` as the sixth positional argument. The new `flusher_processes` parameter is inserted before it, so any existing caller that constructs the factory with `produce_to_pipe` positionally now binds it to `flusher_processes`. The factory then passes the callable to `SpanFlusher` as `max_processes`, where `min(callable, int)` raises a `TypeError` during process count calculation. New parameters should be added after existing ones, or made keyword-only, to preserve the existing call contract.

Negative flusher_processes disables flushing and backpressure silently

`max_processes` comes from the new `--flusher-processes` click option with `type=int` and no range validation. `SpanFlusher` first does `self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)`, so `0` becomes "all shards", but a negative value survives to line 60 where `min(negative, len(shards))` returns a negative number. `range(negative)` then produces an empty `process_to_shards_map`, so no flusher processes or per-process buffers are created. `submit()` still accepts messages: the backpressure and Redis-memory checks iterate over empty `process_backpressure_since` and `self.buffers` collections, so spans continue to be written to Redis while nothing flushes them. This can fill Redis and lead to data loss/consumer failure. Add validation such as `click.IntRange(min=1)` and handle `0` explicitly.

Production multiprocessing flusher path is not tested

Both tests pass `produce_to_pipe=messages.append`, which makes `SpanFlusher._create_process_for_shards` create `threading.Thread` instances instead of the production `mp_context.Process` path with `run_with_initialized_sentry(SpanFlusher.main, shard_buffer)`. The new test only asserts that two thread objects are created and that shards are distributed; it does not submit spans or verify that flushing works across processes. As a result, multiprocess-specific behavior such as pickling the per-shard buffer, process restart/health handling, and `join`/terminate behavior in real spawned processes is not exercised.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent partition insertion can race with commit-loop key iteration

`get_committable_offsets()` iterates over `list(self.all_offsets.keys())` without a global lock. `add_offset()` can concurrently insert a new partition key into the same defaultdict. Mutating a dict while iterating over its keys can raise `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or otherwise produce an inconsistent snapshot), which would interrupt that commit-loop pass. Per-partition locks do not protect the outer key set.

OffsetTracker forgets missing offsets after earlier prefix is committed

After `mark_committed()` removes offsets <= the committed offset, `get_committable_offsets()` uses `start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)`. If offsets 100, 102, and 103 are recorded and 100 is committed, `all_offsets` becomes `{102, 103}`. The next scan starts at 102, so it can commit 103 after 102 and 103 complete even though 101 was never added or processed. This violates the stated rule that all prior offsets must be processed and can skip a genuinely missing message if a real offset gap exists.

Result processor exceptions still mark offsets complete and get committed

In `OrderedQueueWorker.run()`, exceptions from `self.result_processor` are caught and logged, but the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...)`. The commit loop only checks whether offsets are outstanding, so an offset whose processing raised will later be committed as successfully processed. This contradicts the class guarantee that only successful work is committed and can silently drop a message if a result processor ever raises transiently.

Shared FixedQueuePool becomes unusable after strategy close and can drop messages on rebalance

`ResultsStrategyFactory` creates one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__`, and each `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` receives that same pool. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`, which shuts down the queues and workers, but `factory.queue_pool` remains non-None. If Arroyo creates a new strategy from the same factory after a rebalance, the new strategy reuses the shut-down pool. `Queue.put()` on a shut-down queue raises `queue.ShutDown`; `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` catches all exceptions and marks the offset complete, so messages for the new assignment can be silently dropped.

Shutdown stops workers before queued work is drained

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown()` sets each worker's `shutdown` flag before calling `Queue.shutdown(immediate=False)`. `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` checks `while not self.shutdown` at the top of every loop, so a worker that finishes its current item will exit immediately instead of dequeuing the remaining items already in its queue. Since there is exactly one worker per queue, queued work is left unprocessed. This makes the advertised graceful shutdown incorrect and can cause those messages to be delayed or reprocessed after restart/rebalance.

Unbounded queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory

`FixedQueuePool.__init__` creates each work queue with `queue.Queue()` using the default `maxsize=0`, meaning queues are unbounded. The class doc says there is "natural backpressure when queues fill up," but these queues never fill. If workers process more slowly than the consumer submits, both the queues and the offset-tracking sets grow without bound, eventually risking memory exhaustion or very large commit-lag.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Permission denial cache key can collide when name/parent contain underscores

`userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates namespace, UID, action, name, and parent with underscores and no escaping or length delimiter. Dashboard names and folder UIDs can contain underscores, so distinct tuples can produce the same key. For example, `name="a_b", parent="c"` and `name="a", parent="b_c"` both produce a suffix like `dashboards:read_a_b_c`. A cached denial for one resource can therefore be served for a different resource, causing an authorized check to be denied.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous denials can deny renderer access

The denial cache key is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, action, name, and parent folder only. `validateSubject` returns the same UID `"0"` for both `anonymous:0` and `render:0`. If an anonymous check for a dashboard is denied, `permDenialCache` stores a key such as `org-12.perm_0_dashboards:read_dash1_fold1`. A later renderer check for the same dashboard and folder hits this denial entry at line 117 and returns `Allowed: false` before `getRendererPermissions` can grant the renderer wildcard read access. This causes authorized rendering to fail depending on prior anonymous requests.

List treats a cached empty or stale permission map as authoritative and skips DB refresh

`List` only falls back to `getIdentityPermissions` when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error. A cached empty map (`map[string]bool{}`) is a successful cache hit, so `List` passes it directly to `listPermission`. A user who listed dashboards before creating any (or before the new permission was granted) can have an empty/partial `permCache` entry; after creating a dashboard, the next list request will keep returning the stale cached map until the 30s TTL expires. The client-side `NoopCache` change does not help because this is the server-side `permCache`. This undermines the PR goal of letting creators fetch newly created dashboards/folders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem in filtered rule list

In the rules.map branch for origin === 'grafana', the newly rendered GrafanaRuleListItem has no key prop, while the other branches use key={key}. Since this is a React list, the missing key causes index-based reconciliation, which can reuse component state such as open menus or focus for the wrong rule as the list changes and triggers React warnings. Pass key={key} to GrafanaRuleListItem.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence drawer never opens for prom-only Grafana rules

GrafanaRuleListItem now renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule, so rule is undefined. The AlertRuleMenu can show the Silence notifications item based on the promRule ability, and handleSilence sets showSilenceDrawer to true, but this line only renders SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true. With rule undefined, clicking Silence does nothing in the new list view. The condition and drawer data need to support the promRule-only path.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete action is missing for Grafana rules in the alert list view

The Delete Menu.Item is still wrapped in {canDelete && rulerRule && ...}. In the new prom-only alert list view rulerRule is undefined, so Delete never appears even when useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities reports delete as supported and allowed. The actual delete handler passed from RuleActionsButtons already uses only the identifier and groupIdentifier, so the rulerRule guard appears unnecessary and removes delete functionality from the list view.

Duplicate action can appear for data source rules based on Grafana create permission

For a non-Grafana promRule, AlertRuleMenu passes skipToken to useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. However, skipToken is mapped to undefined, and useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined) returns Duplicate as supported with getRulesPermissions('grafana').create as the allowed permission. Because canDuplicate ORs that result with the ruler ability, a data source rule can show the Duplicate menu item even if the user lacks the external write permission required for that rule. This is a UI authorization regression; the backend may still reject the action.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to check isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) before deciding whether update, delete, pause, etc. were supported. After this change it delegates to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which only receives a RulerRuleDTO and a group identifier, and now hardcodes isFederated = false. As a result, federated rule groups can be reported as editable/removable when datasource/folder permissions allow, breaking the previous immutability guard for federated rules.

Pause action is missing for Grafana rules in the alert list view

canPause is now computed from useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities when only promRule is available, but the pause menu item is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) and passes rulerRule to MenuItemPauseRule. In the prom-only alert list view rulerRule is undefined, so the pause action never renders even when canPause is true. Use a pause item that accepts GrafanaPromRuleDTO or derive the required data from promRule, or remove the promRule pause ability if pause is intentionally unsupported.

View link no longer preserves returnTo

The removed GrafanaRuleLoader created the rule view URL with { returnTo: createReturnTo() }. The new GrafanaRuleListItem builds the same /alerting/grafana/${uid}/view URL without returnTo, so navigating from the alert list to a rule and then using in-app back/return controls may no longer return to the previous filtered list. Add returnTo back if list navigation should be preserved.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
$__range queries are now split because interpolation happens before the guard

runSplitQuery() now maps request.targets through datasource.applyTemplateVariables() in the chain ending at line 299, before the querySupportsSplitting() partition on line 300. querySupportsSplitting() deliberately returns false for expressions containing $__range via !isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) (line 287), but by the time it runs, $__range has already been replaced with a concrete duration such as '3d'. The guard is therefore dead. For example, count_over_time({job="x"}[$__range]) over a 3-day window will now be split into one-day subqueries while each subquery still carries the full original range vector, which is not equivalent to the intended single unsplit query and can produce incorrect/duplicated metric results. The range-variable decision must be made on the pre-interpolation expression, or an explicit flag must be preserved; the now-stale comment should also be updated.

Shard splitting interpolates the same queries twice

runShardSplitQuery() interpolates every target at line 52, and the resulting splittingTargets are later used to build subRequest (line 154) and passed to runSplitQuery() (line 163). runSplitQuery() now also applies applyTemplateVariables() to each target in its own pipeline (querySplitting.ts lines 296-299). As a result, every sub-query in the shard-splitting path is interpolated twice; the test in this PR now asserts five applyTemplateVariables calls for a single initial target. Plain substitutions may be harmless, but interpolation is not safely idempotent when a substituted value itself contains template syntax such as $... or [[...]], and it is redundant work otherwise. The shard path should avoid re-interpolating already-interpolated targets, or runSplitQuery should support an already-interpolated/internal entry point.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request completion logs lose traceID field

Previously, logRequest appended traceID from tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) to logParams and imported pkg/infra/tracing. That field and import are removed here. The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware/instrumentContext only adds endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID and uname; it does not add traceID, and m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info has no inherent way to recover it. As a result, every "Plugin Request Completed" log loses trace correlation. If this was not intentional, traceID should be added to the contextual attributes or kept in logParams.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards original logger so log assertions are lost

LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info. TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of returning f or a logger sharing f's Logs. Any test that passes a *TestLogger to NewLoggerMiddleware and then inspects InfoLogs/Calls or Message against that original TestLogger will see zero values, because the actual log was recorded on a fresh, inaccessible TestLogger. Returning f, or otherwise sharing the same counters, would preserve the previous assertion behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to Logger is a source-breaking interface change

Logger is a public interface in pkg/plugins/log. Adding FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger forces every implementation and mock of Logger to implement the new method. This diff updates TestLogger and grafanaInfraLogWrapper, but any other implementation in the repository or any external consumer of this package will fail to compile. If backward compatibility matters, keep Logger unchanged and define a separate optional interface such as ContextualLogger that LoggerMiddleware can type-assert.

No tests cover the new contextual logger behavior

The PR adds ContextualLoggerMiddleware and changes LoggerMiddleware to obtain pluginId, endpoint, user and datasource fields from FromContext(ctx) instead of passing them explicitly. The only test change in the diff renames the metrics test to use newMetricsMiddleware; there is no test that verifies QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth or CollectMetrics adds the expected contextual attributes, nor that LoggerMiddleware actually emits those fields in the completion log. A middleware ordering or context-propagation mistake would not be caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit enforcement is not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit with a separate CountDevices call followed by an insert/upsert, with no transaction, row lock, or serialization. Two different new devices can concurrently both observe count < deviceLimit and both insert, so the stored number of devices can exceed the configured limit. For example, with deviceLimit=1, two concurrent new device requests can both count 0 and both insert, leaving 2 devices.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit can be bypassed by retrying after a rejected tag

In tagDeviceUI, the device ID is written to localCache before CreateOrUpdateDevice is called. If CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached on the first attempt, the cache entry remains. A retry for the same device within the cache TTL hits the cached entry and returns nil before reaching the store, so Anonymous.Authenticate no longer sees ErrDeviceLimitReached and anonymous authentication succeeds. This makes the configured device limit bypassable after one retry, and the rejected device is never recorded.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous authentication now synchronously writes to the device store

Anonymous.Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously on the authentication path. Previously this work was fire-and-forget in a background goroutine. With the default anonymousDeviceLimit=0 this feature is not even active, but every cache-missing anonymous request must still wait for a database upsert before authentication completes. This adds database write latency to anonymous login/page-load paths and is a performance regression for all anonymous traffic.

updateDevice can falsely report ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device

updateDevice treats RowsAffected() == 0 as proof that the device is missing or stale and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL, UPDATE RowsAffected is commonly the number of rows changed, not matched. If an existing row already has the same client_ip, user_agent, and updated_at values (for example, requests within the same second when the timestamp column has second precision), the update can affect 0 rows even though the device exists. The existing device is then rejected and anonymous authentication fails unexpectedly. The code should distinguish 'matched but unchanged' from 'not matched', such as by using CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS or checking existence separately.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine annotation cleanup logs full ID batches at error level

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error after successfully fetching IDs and include the entire ids slice, for example line 534: r.log.Error("Annotations to clean by time", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err). The err variable is nil at that point because errors return early, so this logs every successful batch as an error. The ids slice can be as large as AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, which the new test sets to 32767, so this can flood error logs with large ID lists and impose significant log I/O/CPU. Log successful progress at debug level without dumping all IDs, and reserve error-level logging for actual errors.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute without related rationale

This PR is focused on the annotation cleanup SQL, but this change reduces the top-level cleanup service ticker from every 10 minutes to every 1 minute. That makes all cleanup jobs run ten times as often, which can significantly increase database load and contention, including for the annotation cleanup job this PR is trying to make safer. If this was not intentional, it should be reverted; if it was intentional, it deserves an explicit note in the PR because it is an unrelated behavioral change.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite IN-list construction is quadratic

deleteByIDs builds the inline SQLite ID list with repeated fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v). Each iteration copies the entire accumulated string, making this O(n²) in the number of IDs. For configured batch sizes like the test's 32767, this can copy gigabytes of string data per batch and make cleanup slow or CPU-spiky on SQLite. A strings.Builder or strconv.AppendInt-based construction would avoid the repeated full-string copies.

Subtest cleanup is registered after data creation and initial assertions

In TestIntegrationAnnotationCleanUp, each subtest calls createTestAnnotations and performs initial count assertions before registering the t.Cleanup function that deletes the rows. If any of those early require calls fail, the cleanup is never installed, leaving data in the shared test database and causing later subtests to fail with confusing cascading assertion errors. The t.Cleanup that deletes annotation and annotation_tag rows should be registered before inserting data for the subtest.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
DeleteCollection records legacy duration in the storage metric

In the DeleteCollection goroutine, after d.Legacy.DeleteCollection, the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). This records the legacy operation as a storage operation, corrupting both storage and legacy latency/error metrics and hiding failures in the legacy safety write. It should call d.recordLegacyDuration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records object name in metric kind label

After a successful Storage.Delete, the code calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Every other call passes options.Kind as the third argument. Using the deleted object name as the kind label creates an unbounded Prometheus series per object name, causing high cardinality on delete operations and making the metric impossible to aggregate by resource kind. Pass options.Kind instead of name.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Create uses original obj rather than the object returned by Storage

Create passes the original request obj to d.Legacy.Create instead of the created object returned by d.Storage.Create. If unified storage assigns server-generated fields such as a generated name, UID, or resourceVersion only on the returned object without mutating obj, the legacy write will generate or record a different identity than unified storage. That leaves mode3 with two divergent objects for the same logical create. The legacy writer should receive the object identity returned by unified storage.

Async legacy writes inherit request context and are canceled

In Create (and the same pattern in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135, and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine derives context.WithTimeoutCause from the incoming ctx. In the apiserver this ctx is the request context, which is canceled as soon as the handler returns. Since these legacy writes are scheduled asynchronously after the unified-store write and after the handler returns, they generally start with an already canceled context and are aborted before writing. Mode 3 reads only from unified storage, so legacy is the safety copy; missed legacy creates/updates/deletes can mean lost safety data. Use context.WithoutCancel(ctx) or a fresh background context before adding the timeout.

Legacy update reuses the same UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified-storage result

Update passes the same objInfo to both d.Storage.Update and, asynchronously, d.Legacy.Update. UpdatedObjectInfo.UpdatedObject is invoked independently by each store against its own old object; it is not guaranteed to be idempotent or to produce the same object when legacy is stale. The previous implementation wrapped the object returned from unified storage before sending it to legacy, which ensured both stores wrote the same updated object. Without that, legacy may store a different version from unified storage, defeating the safety copy and potentially causing legacy update failures.

Mode3 integration test asserts immediate legacy consistency after async writes

The new mode3 cases run doPlaylistTests, where k8s create/update/delete now propagate to legacy asynchronously. The test immediately queries the legacy /api/playlists endpoint at line 523 and uses getFromBothAPIs around lines 535 and 547 without waiting or polling for the async legacy write to finish. This makes the mode3 integration tests racy: they can fail when the goroutine has not completed, or pass while the legacy safety write is actually broken. The test should poll or otherwise await eventual convergence before asserting legacy state.

Mode3 unit tests do not wait for or assert legacy writes

The Mode3 Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection tests launch asynchronous legacy writes but do not wait for the goroutines and do not assert that Legacy.Create, Legacy.Update, Legacy.Delete, or Legacy.DeleteCollection were called. An implementation could skip the legacy write entirely and these tests would still pass, and the current context-cancellation issue would not be detected. Add a wait mechanism and assertions for the expected legacy calls.

Storage create/update failures are recorded as legacy duration

On a failed Storage.Create, line 45 calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage), and the same occurs for Storage.Update at line 129. No legacy operation was attempted in these paths, and startStorage measures the unified-store call. This records storage failures and latency in the legacy metric while leaving the storage metric missing those failures. These paths should call recordStorageDuration, and recordLegacyDuration should be used only after actual Legacy calls.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing recheck after write lock causes cache stampede and can clobber a valid cache

After the initial RLock snapshot, the function may see a nil cache and move to the write lock, but it does not re-read entryPointAssetsCache after acquiring that lock. In non-development mode, multiple callers that saw nil on first request can serialize on the write lock and each rebuild the manifest. Worse, if a later rebuild fails, line 69 assigns entryPointAssetsCache = nil, overwriting a valid cache installed by the first caller with nil. Re-check the cache under the write lock in non-dev mode and return the existing value, and avoid replacing an existing valid cache with nil on an error.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lock change allows duplicate concurrent builds for the same index key

`BuildIndex` no longer holds `cacheMu` for the whole build, only when inserting into the cache. However, `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` still performs a non-atomic `GetIndex` then `build`. Two callers for the same missing key can therefore enter `BuildIndex` concurrently. For file-backed indexes both can call `bleve.New` on the same directory and build the same index, causing open/create contention; the loser remains open/leaked and whichever finishes last wins the cache. Distinct keys can be built in parallel, but same-key builds need a per-key lock or singleflight.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
Data race in concurrent index build goroutines

The worker goroutines started by `errgroup` concurrently write shared variables: `totalBatchesIndexed++` on line 189 and `_, _, err = s.build(...)` on line 190, where `err` is the outer function variable. These unsynchronized writes race under the Go race detector, can lose increments for the span event count, and make the code's behavior undefined. Use a local error variable inside each closure and update the counter safely (or compute it after `Wait`).

Events between index build and watch start are dropped

`init` builds each index from storage (`s.build` on line 190) but discards the per-resource resource version returned by `s.build`, then starts `WatchWriteEvents` only after all builds complete (line 203). The SQL backend's `WatchWriteEvents` starts from the latest RV at the time it is called. Any write that commits after the list query for a resource but before this watch start is neither included in the built index nor delivered on the new watch channel, leaving the search index permanently stale for that event until a full rebuild. This is especially likely now that init runs as a blocking startup step while other instances may write.

Search watch goroutine can panic on closed event channel

The watch goroutine receives with `v := <-events` without checking whether the channel is closed. The SQL backend poller closes its event channel when it exits on Stop, so this loop will receive a nil `*WrittenEvent` and call `s.handleEvent(watchctx, v)`, which dereferences `evt.Type` and panics. The goroutine also uses `context.Background()` rather than a cancellable context, so it cannot be stopped by server shutdown. Because `NewResourceServer` now eagerly calls `s.Init`, this goroutine is always started. Use the server/backend context for cancellation and check `v, ok := <-events`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:

CryptoProvider is a public interface. Adding a new abstract method is a binary and source compatibility break for any implementation outside this repository compiled against an older Keycloak version; such providers will fail to compile or can throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader invokes order(). Since this is only used to sort providers, it should have a default implementation (e.g. return 0).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA DER-to-RS conversion silently truncates oversized integers

integerToBytes copies only the low qLength bytes when BigInteger.toByteArray() is longer than the field length. For a DER INTEGER that does not fit in signLength/2 bytes, this discards significant high-order bytes instead of rejecting the malformed/non-canonical signature. That can turn an invalid oversized r or s into a different value and should throw an IOException unless the only extra byte is a leading zero sign byte.

The test signs data, converts DER to concatenated RS, back to DER, then back to concatenated RS, and only asserts the two raw RS arrays are equal. The test also uses the same default EC key pair for ES256, ES384, and ES512 instead of curve/key sizes matching each algorithm.

Equal-order server crypto providers are silently selected instead of rejected

If e.g. the default and FIPS provider are accidentally both on the classpath, ServiceLoader iteration order determines which one is used, so a non-FIPS provider may be selected in a FIPS environment instead of failing fast. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
V2 authorization cleanup is skipped on role/client/group removal

The listener now runs its cleanup only when the legacy ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is enabled. When ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled by itself, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, but this block does not execute, so client/role/group removal does not clean up the corresponding admin-permission resources or policies in V2. true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission can return the all-clients resource name as a client ID

getClientsWithPermission iterates over every resource of type CLIENTS, including the special all-clients resource whose name is AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE ("Clients"). If hasGrantedPermission() is true for that resource, the code adds resource.getName() to a set that callers treat as actual client IDs. With a type-level "all clients" permission the returned set contains "Clients" instead of all real client IDs, so callers filtering clients can end up with no matching clients or a bogus client ID. The all-resource case must be expanded to actual client IDs or otherwise handled explicitly, and the resource-type resource name must not be returned as a client ID.

Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

As a result, an administrator holding the realm manage-clients role but no explicit fine-grained map-roles/map-roles-composite/map-roles-client-scope permission is denied these client role operations when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. For a policy with resource type Clients, including the all-clients resource, it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is null for these resources or at best the raw client UUID, and it never returns an "All clients"-style display. This leaves the new client resource type without a proper human-readable resource name in permission representations. A CLIENTS branch symmetric to USERS is needed, resolving client IDs to clientId and mapping the type resource to a display such as "All clients".

Caution overstates when the operator will fail without rolling-updates

The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
